reviewer: one read-through of all 79 outputs by an AI model (Claude Opus 5.5) after the run, comparing each output with its canonical entry. Not a clinician, pharmacist or teacher review; the domain calls below have not been confirmed by a human expert.
scope: All 79 final outputs were read, not just the sample. Calls: agree, verifier miss (accepted output contains a claim judged wrong), probable verifier miss, debatable, canonical error inherited (the error is in the seed text, which the verifier treats as ground truth), questionable reject.

ai-agent::nurse::final.note: Keeps goal, tool call, read result, loop. The vendor example is a plausible agent workflow.

aid-accuracy::pharmacist::final.note: The drug-interaction version of the always-"no" example is correct: most arbitrary drug pairs have no clinically significant interaction, so a constant "no interaction" answer scores well and misses the real ones.

aid-parameters::pharmacist::final.note: "smaller than Claude" asserts a parameter count Anthropic has not published, and "light enough to run on a laptop" holds only for high-memory laptops with a quantized model. Both come from the canonical example sentence, so the verifier, which checks against the canonical, cannot catch them.

cloud-alert::nurse::final.note: Pump alarms, nuisance alarms and alarm fatigue are real and correctly described.

cloud-cdn::teacher::final.note: Accurate; the stale-copy explanation matches how CDN caching behaves.

data-backfill::pharmacist::final.note: Accurate. The light comparison to correcting dispensed or billed records is fair.

sec-mfa::nurse::final.note: Accurate; keeps "two or more kinds of proof".

sec-rbac::teacher::final.note: Accurate; roles carry permissions, users inherit them.

sys-http-response::pharmacist::final.note: Status code, headers and body preserved. Minor: many pharmacy claims travel over the NCPDP telecommunication standard through a switch rather than a plain HTTP API, but the sentence is still plausible for a modern integration.

sys-http-header::nurse::pass1.note: Correct rejection. SBAR is a handoff communication format, not a label stapled to a chart. The retry dropped the analogy and was accepted.

sys-jwt::teacher::pass1.note: The only failed criterion was example_reads_natural, citing the capital "The" at the start of the example. Accepted outputs in the same run also start with capitals (for example ai-agent::nurse and aid-ai::teacher), so the rule was applied inconsistently. The rejection doubled the run cost (about $0.21 against $0.10).

bi-rls::nurse::final.note: The analogy says a nurse "can only open charts for patients on your unit, not the whole hospital: the system knows who you are and hides the rest." In typical hospital EHRs, clinicians can open other patients' charts; access is controlled mainly by audit and break-the-glass policies, not by hiding rows. The verifier passed analogy_target_accurate with "EHRs do restrict chart access by unit/assignment; the claim is factually true in nursing practice", which is the error itself.

cloud-environment::pharmacist::final.note: The example sentence says the bug "only shows up in the staging environment because that's the only place connected to the real insurance claim system." That is backwards: production is the environment connected to real external systems, and the output's own definition says so. technical_accuracy_preserved passed.

bi-rls::pharmacist::final.note: "your pharmacy system only shows a tech the patients and queues tied to their store, not every store in the chain." Work queues are store-scoped, but chain pharmacy systems usually share patient profiles across stores (that is how transfers and refills at another location work). The verifier accepted the claim as accurate.

sys-jwt::pharmacist::final.note: "a signed, tamper-evident script label" is not a real pharmacy artifact. Tamper-resistance requirements apply to written prescription pads, not dispensing labels, and labels carry no signature that proves they were not altered. The verifier reasoned that labels "can carry tamper-evident features", which conflates the two.

sec-oauth::pharmacist::final.note: The prescription-transfer analogy says the other pharmacy hands over records but "never the patient's login to their chart". Patients have no login to a pharmacy's dispensing record, so the contrast the analogy depends on does not exist, and a transfer is a pharmacist-to-pharmacist exchange, not a token issued by a third party after user consent. The mapping is loose on both sides.

sec-mfa::pharmacist::final.note: "the same reason a C-II dispense needs more than one check" maps MFA to multiple checks, but MFA's point is different kinds of proof; two passwords are not MFA. The verifier's own worked example (double-counting does not model idempotence) describes this failure mode.

sys-http-header::pharmacist::final.note: The "label stapled to a prescription bag" carrying prescriber, fill date and warnings mixes up the bag label or receipt with the vial label and auxiliary warning labels. Structurally fine, but a pharmacist would notice the detail.

sys-payload::nurse::final.note: Calls the shift, room number and sender the "wrapper" around SBAR content, but patient identification and location are part of SBAR's Situation, not packaging around it.

bi-calculated-column::nurse::final.note: "if you use a column where you needed a measure, your totals won't update when the user changes the view." A calculated column aggregated in a visual does respond to slicers; what stays fixed is the per-row value and anything computed per row (such as a ratio). The claim is in the canonical why_it_matters and appears in all three renderings of this term.

extra: Verifier strictness: technical_accuracy_preserved and analogy_target_accurate failed 0 times in 78 parsed first-pass verdicts, while this read-through found 2 clear and 3 probable wrong claims among 78 accepted outputs. Four of the five are in analogies (18 accepted outputs used one), so the analogy side is where the verifier is weakest.

The pharmacist profile accounts for 4 of the 5 flagged misses and 2 of the 3 debatable accepts. Part of that may be where claims were easiest to check, so the nurse and teacher outputs should not be read as clean.

The one fallback (aid-accuracy::teacher) was a Pass 1 JSON parse failure, not a verifier rejection. The function logs only the first 200 characters of unparseable output, and this run stored the same, so the cause could not be established. The runner now keeps the full raw text for parse failures.
